rationale: A wins because it makes the missing customer proof part of the story instead of hiding it: "Skydio's inspection drone flies power lines with nobody at the controls — and no named utility willing to say so" is sharp, skeptical, and immediately pitch-shaped. B is competent, but "Skydio's pilotless inspection drone wants to take the lineworker off the truck" smuggles in a labor-and-truck replacement story the update does not give you. Both sets need cleanup, but A has the colder editorial spine and the better refusal discipline.
gaps_in_A: "A US drone maker bets the grid will pay a premium to avoid Chinese hardware" invents the premium. The update gives US-made positioning against Chinese drone makers, not buyer willingness to pay more.
"no named utility willing to say so" turns nondisclosure into motive. The fact is only that no named utility was disclosed.
"the defect report arrives without a human in the loop" overstates the automation. The update says reports are sent automatically; it does not say no human reviews or approves them.
gaps_in_B: "take the lineworker off the truck" invents the lineworker and truck frame. The update says no pilot, not displaced field crews.
"the operational shift from a crewed inspection truck to a docked drone" repeats the same unsupported replacement claim inside the angle body.
"category-creation" and "autonomous grid inspection category" inflate a product launch into a category story before the set has customer proof, market data, or named deployments.
"enterprise-tech reporter" is weaker journalist shape than the rest of the set. It is narrowed later, but the label starts too broad for a founder actually building a list.
